children: The Defence Minister highlights the push for indigenous capabilities as defence production reaches Rs 1.78 lakh crore in 2025-26
India is focusing on strengthening its domestic defence ecosystem to reduce dependence on foreign sources and address national security challenges, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said on Tuesday.

Addressing a meeting of the Defence Ministry’s Consultative Committee in Jaisalmer, Singh said strategic autonomy and indigenous technological capabilities were essential to safeguarding national security. He added that the government had been supporting the domestic defence industry as part of its efforts to reduce the country's reliance on overseas suppliers.
The meeting discussed emerging security challenges, changes in warfare, technological developments and the need to prepare the armed forces for evolving operational requirements.
Singh said the defence budget for the financial year 2026-27 had been increased to a record Rs 7.85 lakh crore, including a capital outlay of Rs 2.19 lakh crore.

He highlighted the government's focus on budgetary support and capital acquisition to meet the modernisation requirements of the armed forces. He also stressed the need to ensure that financial resources were effectively utilised and allocated according to the services' critical requirements.

Defence production increased from Rs 46,429 crore in 2014-15 to a record Rs 1.78 lakh crore in 2025-26, Singh said. Defence exports, which were below Rs 2,000 crore in 2014, had risen to around Rs 40,000 crore.
The government aims to achieve defence production worth Rs 3 lakh crore and exports worth Rs 50,000 crore by 2029, he added.

Singh said technological developments were changing the nature of warfare and that the armed forces needed to adapt to emerging operational requirements. He also emphasised the importance of human capital, stating that military preparedness depended not only on technology and financial resources but also on the capabilities and readiness of personnel.
He said all three services had been refining their structures and formations in response to changing warfare requirements.

Referring to the Indian Army's new formations, Singh said the Asani, Bhairav and Shaktiban platoons were addressing contemporary operational requirements and adapting to changing battlefield conditions.

The discussions also focused on accelerating the induction of next-generation platforms and weapon systems, strengthening integration among the three services, and improving joint operational planning and coordination.
Singh said defence modernisation was a continuous process that required sustained efforts to maintain operational preparedness amid evolving technologies and security challenges.

According to the Defence Ministry, the meeting emphasised the need to translate modernisation plans into implementation through a structured and phased approach. The objective is to build a military capable of responding to conventional, sub-conventional and multi-domain security challenges.
